title: A brighter decade? One area, 2014–2024
selectionReason: Demo content — replace with verified public data. Record why this place was chosen, who chose it, and whether people connected to it were consulted.
question: Observed night-time light in this area changed over ten years. What could that mean — and what can it not tell us?
summary: This demo case study shows how the observatory presents one area's night-time-light record. The numbers are illustrative placeholders, shaped to show a typical pattern: a general rise, a dip, and a year with no usable value.

dataset.name: VIIRS Nighttime Lights (VNL), annual composites — intended source
dataset.provider: Earth Observation Group, Payne Institute for Public Policy, Colorado School of Mines
dataset.resolution: 15 arc-second grid — roughly 450–500 m across near the equator. One cell can cover several streets, fields, or a whole village.
dataset.unit: nW/cm²/sr (nanowatts per square centimetre per steradian)
dataset.temporalAggregation: One value per year, built from many night-time passes
dataset.processingSummary: Demo summary — confirm against provider documentation. Annual products are assembled from many nightly observations after screening for cloud, moonlight, stray light and other effects. For this case study, the values would then be averaged over the selected area.
dataset.license: To be confirmed on the provider page before publication

coverage.explanation: Demo content. Some years in this series are marked limited or unknown to show how the observatory discloses uneven coverage. In a verified case study, this label would come from the product's cloud-free / valid-observation counts.
coverage.validObservationNote: Demo content — replace with the number of valid (cloud-free) observations per year from the source product.

comparison.note: Conceptual comparison generated for the demo. It is not a map of real pixel values and does not show any real place.
comparison.cellSizeLabel: Each square stands in for one ~500 m grid cell

observedChange.statement: Observed average radiance in the selected area increased between 2014 and 2023, with a dip in 2020. No usable value is available for 2024 in this demo series.
observedChange.caveat: This does not establish why it changed or what that change meant for people living there.

limitations: Annual composites can hide short-lived events such as outages, festivals, or seasonal activity.
Products are corrected for cloud, moonlight, snow, stray light and other effects; those corrections can differ between years and product versions.
Spatial resolution is coarse: one grid cell can mix homes, roads, industry and open land.
Light can come from many sources — streets, vehicles, industry, fires, gas flares — not only homes.
A change in lighting technology (for example, a switch to LEDs) can change the recorded value without any change in activity.
